blocks.text: A systems program can return the right number while leaking its descriptor. It can protect a variable with an atomic operation while leaving the surrounding object lifetime unsafe. It can accept a network request while retaining more work than it can process. Systems programming begins where a language-level operation meets a resource, timing, representation, or failure boundary that the application cannot ignore.

blocks.text: This volume follows the fictional HarborWorks engineering team as it develops tools and a local request service. The setting connects object representation, resource ownership, native I/O, processes, protocols, concurrency, and shutdown through recurring engineering questions. The examples are original educational scenarios, not descriptions of an employer’s infrastructure or production software. No classified systems or confidential implementation details are used.

topics.title: Technical scope and source boundaries
topics.summary: The common language baseline is C++20. The standard-library chapters use facilities available in that baseline, while native examples are explicitly targeted at Linux or the marked POSIX interface. Linux-specific descriptor flags, process inspection, shared-memory setup, and socket behavior are not presented as portable Windows or macOS APIs. A portable class interface does not make its native implementation platform-independent.

blocks.text: The capstone is a bounded loopback teaching service, not a certified production daemon. It deliberately lacks peer authentication, TLS, internet exposure, durable transactions, deployment supervision, and a hard-real-time scheduling analysis. Its explicit request deadlines and queue bounds are useful engineering mechanisms within stated limits, not a guarantee that an ordinary operating system will meet every wall-clock deadline under arbitrary load.

topics.title: Read for a decision, then trace the mechanism
topics.summary: Before entering a command or copying a function, identify the requirement it serves. Ask who owns each resource, which objects are borrowed, what operation can fail, and what evidence would establish completion. A successful allocation does not establish object initialization. A successful connection does not establish application acceptance. A stop request does not establish that a worker has exited.

topics.title: Keep the lab bounded
topics.summary: Use an ordinary unprivileged account in a disposable development environment. Network examples bind IPv4 loopback and use selected local ports; they do not contact external services or change firewall policy. File fixtures use owned temporary locations or explicitly marked scratch resources. Process examples launch their own controlled executable or perform a small single-threaded fork exercise.

topics.title: Interpret output at the correct level
topics.summary: Addresses, PIDs, selected ports, layout measurements, timings, and lock-free observations can vary. Tests assert the intended relationships rather than one particular machine’s incidental values. A printed elapsed duration is not a benchmark conclusion unless the workload and measurement method support that conclusion. A sanitizer-clean execution is evidence about the paths executed, not exhaustive proof of safety.

topics.title: The central operating rule
topics.summary: Establish ownership before use, validate before mutation, synchronize before observation, and make cleanup possible before starting concurrent work. Carry that rule from the first descriptor wrapper to the final server. A system is understandable when a reviewer can trace both its successful request path and its failed startup, truncated input, cancellation, and shutdown paths without guessing who still owns the resources.
